title: Single-Gene Neurodevelopmental Syndromes
summary: Classic monogenic disorders that reveal how specific proteins control neuronal growth and synapses.

lessons.title: Fragile X Syndrome and FMRP

levels.kid:
Inside every cell is a giant instruction book called DNA. One page of that book holds the recipe for a helper protein called **FMRP**.

FMRP works like a traffic cop at the tiny connections between brain cells. It tells the cell, "Slow down! Don't build too many parts at once."

In **Fragile X syndrome**, one tiny word on that page gets repeated over and over, like a stuck record: CGG, CGG, CGG... When it repeats too many times, the cell shuts the page and stops making FMRP.

Without the traffic cop, brain connections get messy. Children with Fragile X may learn more slowly, feel worried in busy places, and find loud sounds too much. With good support, they learn, grow, and enjoy life.
levels.hs:
**Fragile X syndrome (FXS)** is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability, and the most common known single-gene cause of autism. It affects roughly 1 in 4,000 males and 1 in 8,000 females.

The cause is a change in the **FMR1 gene** on the X chromosome. This gene has a short stretch where three DNA letters, **CGG**, are repeated. Most people have about 5-44 repeats. When the repeat grows past **200**, it is called a **full mutation**. The cell then adds chemical tags (**methylation**) that switch the gene off, so no **FMRP** protein is made.

FMRP binds messenger RNA at synapses and acts as a brake on protein production. Without it, synapses make too many proteins and stay immature.

Because FMR1 is on the X chromosome, boys (XY) are usually more strongly affected than girls (XX), who have a second, often working copy.

Common features include:
- Intellectual disability and learning difficulties
- Anxiety, social avoidance, poor eye contact, and autism features
- Sensitivity to sound and touch
- A long face, large ears, and in teens, enlarged testes

The repeat can grow when passed from mother to child. A mother with a **premutation** (55-200 repeats) may have a child with the full mutation. This growth from one generation to the next is called **anticipation**. Diagnosis uses a DNA test that counts the repeats.
levels.college:
FXS is an X-linked **trinucleotide repeat disorder** caused, in more than 99% of cases, by expansion of a CGG repeat in the 5' untranslated region of **FMR1** (Xq27.3).

**Allele classes** (repeat number):
- Normal: about 5-44, usually with AGG interruptions every 9-10 CGGs that stabilize the repeat
- Intermediate (gray zone): 45-54
- **Premutation**: 55-200
- **Full mutation**: >200, leading to hypermethylation of the repeat and the FMR1 promoter, heterochromatin formation, and **transcriptional silencing**

The name comes from a **fragile site** seen on karyotype when cells are grown in folate-deficient medium. Today diagnosis relies on PCR with Southern blot, or repeat-primed PCR, to size the repeat and assess methylation.

**Inheritance.** Expansion from premutation to full mutation happens almost only during **maternal transmission**. The risk rises with maternal repeat size and falls with the number of AGG interruptions. Fathers with a premutation pass it to all daughters, generally without major expansion.

**FMRP function.** FMRP is an RNA-binding protein with KH domains and an RGG box. It associates with polyribosomes and represses translation of hundreds of dendritic mRNAs, including PSD-95, Arc, CaMKIIα and MAP1B. Synaptic activity, especially group I metabotropic glutamate receptor (**mGluR5**) signaling, normally relieves this repression locally.

**Consequences of FMRP loss:**
- Excess basal protein synthesis at synapses
- Long, thin, immature **dendritic spines** at higher density (seen in human postmortem tissue and in Fmr1 knockout mice)
- Exaggerated mGluR-dependent long-term depression (LTD)
- Cortical hyperexcitability, so seizures occur in a minority of patients

**Clinical picture.** Males: moderate intellectual disability, ADHD-like symptoms, hyperarousal, anxiety, autism (about 30-60%), macroorchidism after puberty, and connective-tissue laxity. Females with a full mutation vary widely depending on **X-inactivation** skew.

Premutation carriers have distinct risks that come from a different mechanism, discussed below.
levels.phd:
The **mGluR theory** (Bear, Huber and Warren, 2004) proposed that many FXS phenotypes stem from unchecked protein synthesis downstream of group I mGluRs. Huber et al. (2002) showed enhanced, protein-synthesis-independent mGluR-LTD in hippocampal CA1 of Fmr1 KO mice. Dölen et al. (2007) found that halving mGluR5 (Grm5+/-) rescued spine density, audiogenic seizures, and other phenotypes in KO mice. This was a landmark genetic rescue.

**Mechanism of translational control.** Darnell et al. (2011) used HITS-CLIP to identify about 842 FMRP target transcripts, enriched for synaptic and autism-risk genes. FMRP binds these mostly in coding regions and appears to stall ribosomes during elongation, rather than blocking initiation. A complementary model involves **CYFIP1**, which binds FMRP and the cap-binding protein eIF4E, acting as a 4E-BP-like inhibitor. FMRP also interacts with microRNA machinery. In addition, it has translation-independent roles:
- Direct binding to channels such as Slack (KCNT1), BK channels and Kv4
- Regulation of action potential duration and presynaptic release

Loss of FMRP therefore produces a channelopathy component alongside synaptic dysregulation. Downstream signaling is dysregulated too, with elevated **ERK1/2** and **PI3K-mTOR** activity and increased **MMP-9**.

**Premutation pathology works differently.** Premutation alleles show elevated FMR1 mRNA (2-8 fold) with modestly reduced FMRP. Two mechanisms drive toxicity:
- **RNA gain-of-function**: CGG-repeat RNA sequesters proteins such as Sam68 and DROSHA/DGCR8
- **Repeat-associated non-AUG (RAN) translation** produces the toxic polyglycine peptide **FMRpolyG**, found in intranuclear inclusions

These mechanisms underlie **FXTAS** (fragile X-associated tremor/ataxia syndrome), a late-onset neurodegeneration more common in older male carriers, and **FXPOI** (primary ovarian insufficiency, about 20% of female carriers).

**Silencing mechanics.** In full mutations, the expanded CGG RNA can hybridize to the DNA as an R-loop. This structure is linked to epigenetic silencing beginning around the end of the first trimester in human embryonic tissue. **Mosaicism** for repeat size or methylation, and partially unmethylated full mutations, correlate with milder cognition, which shows that residual FMRP level is the key determinant of severity.
levels.expert:
**Translational failure.** FXS became a cautionary tale for translational neuroscience. Mouse-validated mGluR5 negative allosteric modulators, **mavoglurant** (AFQ056, Novartis) and **basimglurant** (Roche), failed their primary endpoints in large placebo-controlled trials of adolescents and adults around 2014-2016. Arbaclofen, a GABA-B agonist, also missed its primary endpoint, though post hoc signals in social avoidance prompted renewed studies.

Lessons drawn from these failures:
- Behavioral rating scales were noisy and showed large placebo responses.
- Treatment started late in development, when circuits may be less plastic.
- Animals developed tolerance in some chronic dosing paradigms.
- Patients were not stratified, so mosaics and partially methylated cases were mixed with fully silenced ones.

The field has since prioritized objective biomarkers: EEG resting gamma power (elevated in FXS and in KO mice), auditory chirp-evoked phase locking, eye tracking, and quantitative FMRP assays in blood. The Fragile X Clinical and Research Consortium registry (FORWARD) supports natural-history data.

**Current directions:**
- **PDE4D inhibition**: zatolmilast (BPN14770) aims to restore cAMP signaling, which is reduced in FXS. Phase 2 suggested cognitive benefit, prompting phase 3 trials.
- **Cannabidiol** transdermal gel (Zygel) did not meet its primary endpoint overall. A subgroup with full methylation looked more responsive, which led to a confirmatory trial.
- **Gene reactivation**: CRISPR-dCas9-Tet1 targeted demethylation reactivated FMR1 in patient-derived neurons and rescued engrafted cells (Liu et al., 2018). Excising the expanded repeat also derepresses the gene. In vivo delivery remains the barrier.
- **Minocycline**, an MMP-9 inhibitor, gave modest trial benefits but has limited enthusiasm because of its side effects.

**Clinical pitfalls.** Large-scale repeat-primed PCR can miss methylation status, and chromosomal microarray and standard exome sequencing do not reliably detect repeat expansions. Fragile X testing should therefore be ordered specifically in unexplained intellectual disability or autism. Rare FMR1 deletions or point mutations (for example R138Q) cause FXS-like phenotypes without expansion, so sequencing is needed if repeat testing is normal but suspicion is high. Cascade testing of relatives matters: identifying a premutation has implications for FXTAS, FXPOI and FXAND (associated neuropsychiatric disorders) across generations.

**Open question.** Is FMRP restoration in adolescence or adulthood sufficient, or is there a closing critical window? Inducible-rescue mouse data suggest substantial adult reversibility for some phenotypes, not all.

keyPoints: Fragile X is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability
Caused by >200 CGG repeats in FMR1 that silence the gene by methylation
FMRP is an RNA-binding brake on local synaptic protein synthesis
FMRP loss gives immature dendritic spines and exaggerated mGluR-LTD
Premutation (55-200 repeats) causes FXTAS and FXPOI by RNA toxicity
mGluR5 drugs worked in mice but failed in human trials

test.q: Which gene is mutated in Fragile X syndrome?
test.explain: FMR1 on Xq27.3 encodes FMRP. MECP2 causes Rett syndrome, and TSC2 causes tuberous sclerosis.

test.q: What repeat number defines a full mutation in FMR1?
test.explain: More than 200 CGG repeats leads to methylation and silencing. 55-200 repeats is a premutation.

test.q: How does a full mutation stop FMRP production?
choices: It methylates and silences the gene
It removes the whole X chromosome

test.q: What is FMRP's main job at synapses?
choices: Pumping sodium out of the neuron
test.explain: FMRP is an RNA-binding protein that acts as a brake on local protein synthesis at synapses.

test.q: Dendritic spines in Fragile X brains tend to be:
test.explain: Postmortem tissue and knockout mice show dense, long, thin, immature spines.

test.q: Why are boys usually more severely affected than girls?
choices: The repeat expands faster in sons
Boys have one X with no backup copy
Girls make more FMRP on chromosome 21
test.explain: Males have a single X. Females have a second, often normal copy, and their severity depends on X-inactivation.

test.q: Expansion to a full mutation happens mainly during:
test.explain: Premutations expand to full mutations almost only when passed through the mother.

test.q: Which receptor's signaling is exaggerated in the mGluR theory?
test.explain: Group I mGluR (mGluR5) signaling and the resulting LTD are excessive when FMRP's brake is missing.

test.q: FXTAS mainly affects which group?
test.explain: FXTAS is a late-onset tremor/ataxia syndrome caused by premutation RNA toxicity, most common in older men.

test.q: The repeated DNA triplet in Fragile X is ___.
test.explain: CGG repeats in the 5' UTR of FMR1 expand in Fragile X.

test.q: What is the term for 55-200 CGG repeats?
test.explain: Premutation carriers make FMRP but are at risk for FXTAS and FXPOI and can pass on expansions.

test.q: When a disorder becomes more severe, starts earlier, or affects more family members in successive generations, this phenomenon is called ___.
test.explain: Anticipation is the clinical pattern of increasing severity, earlier onset or higher risk in later generations. In fragile X, it reflects CGG repeat expansion (a dynamic mutation): an unstable premutation can expand to a full mutation, mainly on maternal transmission. This explains the Sherman paradox.

kidTest.q: What does the protein FMRP do in the brain?
kidTest.explain: FMRP tells brain connections to slow down building parts.

kidTest.q: What goes wrong in the Fragile X gene?
choices: A tiny word repeats too much
kidTest.explain: CGG repeats too many times, and the gene shuts off.

kidTest.q: What might feel too much for kids with Fragile X?
kidTest.explain: Many kids with Fragile X are sensitive to loud sounds.

kidTest.q: What helps kids with Fragile X do well?
kidTest.explain: With good support, they learn and grow.

kidTest.q: The instruction book inside cells is D _ _.
kidTest.explain: DNA holds the recipes for proteins like FMRP.

advancedTest.q: Halving mGluR5 rescued Fmr1 KO phenotypes (Dölen 2007). What did this most directly support?
choices: Excess group I mGluR signaling drives many FXS features
FXS is caused by too little synaptic protein synthesis
FMRP loss acts mainly by blocking NMDA receptors
Spine defects come from premutation RNA toxicity
advancedTest.explain: Genetic reduction of mGluR5 counteracting the phenotypes supports the mGluR theory of unchecked downstream synthesis.

advancedTest.q: Why do premutation carriers develop FXTAS even though they make FMRP?
choices: They lose their second X chromosome
Their FMRP is fully silenced by methylation
Excess CGG RNA and RAN peptides are toxic
advancedTest.explain: Premutations raise FMR1 mRNA, causing RNA gain-of-function and FMRpolyG toxicity, a mechanism distinct from FMRP loss.

advancedTest.q: A boy with a full mutation is milder than expected. What is the likeliest explanation?
choices: Skewed X-inactivation on his single X
An extra copy of mGluR5 from his father
Higher AGG interruptions in his mother's allele
Methylation mosaicism leaving some FMRP made
advancedTest.explain: Partially unmethylated or mosaic alleles allow residual FMRP, which tracks severity. X-inactivation does not apply to a male's single X.

advancedTest.q: Which change would best address a key reason the mGluR5 trials failed?
choices: Using objective biomarkers like EEG gamma power
Restricting trials to older adults with long exposure
Dropping placebo groups to cut the trial size
Enrolling mosaics and full methylators together
advancedTest.explain: Noisy rating scales and placebo response undermined the trials, so objective biomarkers and stratification are now prioritized.

lessons.title: Rett Syndrome and MECP2

levels.kid:
Imagine a baby girl who grows and learns just like other babies. She smiles, grabs toys and starts saying words. Then, around her first or second birthday, something changes. She slowly loses some words and stops using her hands to hold things. Instead, her hands move together over and over, like washing or clapping.

This is called **Rett syndrome**. It happens because of a change in one gene, called **MECP2**. A gene is like a recipe card in your cells.

The MECP2 recipe makes a helper that works like a volume knob for many other genes in brain cells. When the knob is broken, brain cells can't fine-tune their messages.

Here is the hopeful part. In mice, scientists fixed the gene later in life, and the mice got much better!
levels.hs:
**Rett syndrome** is a neurodevelopmental disorder that mostly affects girls, roughly 1 in 10,000 female births. It is caused by mutations in **MECP2**, a gene on the **X chromosome**.

The typical story has stages:
- From birth to about 6 to 18 months, development seems normal.
- Then comes **regression**: the child loses spoken words and purposeful hand use.
- Repetitive **hand stereotypies** appear, such as hand-wringing, clapping or mouthing.
- Walking problems, breathing irregularities (breath-holding or over-breathing), seizures, scoliosis and slowed head growth often follow.
- The condition then stabilizes. It is not a steady decline like dementia.

Why mostly girls? Girls have two X chromosomes. In each cell, one X is randomly switched off (**X-inactivation**), so a girl with one mutated copy has a mix of healthy and affected cells. Boys have only one X, so a severe mutation usually causes a much more serious brain disease in infancy.

Most cases are **de novo**, meaning the mutation is new in the child and not inherited. It usually arises in the father's sperm.

MECP2 makes a protein that binds to chemically tagged (methylated) DNA and helps control which genes neurons turn on and off. In 2007, Adrian Bird's lab showed that switching the gene back on in adult Rett mice reversed many symptoms. That changed how scientists think about the disorder.
levels.college:
**Rett syndrome (RTT)** was described by Andreas Rett in 1966. In 1999, Huda Zoghbi's lab (Amir et al.) identified **MECP2** (Xq28) as the cause. About 95% of classic RTT cases carry a pathogenic MECP2 variant.

**Clinical diagnosis** (2010 revised criteria) requires a period of regression followed by recovery or stabilization, plus these main criteria:
- Partial or complete loss of purposeful hand skills
- Partial or complete loss of spoken language
- Gait abnormalities (dyspraxic gait or inability to walk)
- Stereotypic hand movements

Supportive features include breathing dysregulation while awake, bruxism, impaired sleep, abnormal muscle tone, scoliosis, small cold hands and feet, and intense eye communication. Deceleration of head growth is common, but it is no longer required for diagnosis. **Atypical RTT** variants include a preserved-speech (Zappella) form, and other genes produce related pictures: **CDKL5** (early-onset seizures) and **FOXG1** (congenital form).

**The protein.** MeCP2 has a **methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD)** and a **transcriptional repressor domain (TRD)**. The TRD contains the **NCoR/SMRT interaction domain (NID)**. MeCP2 is extremely abundant in mature neurons, about as common as histone octamers. It binds methylated cytosines and recruits the NCoR/SMRT co-repressor complex with HDAC3.

**Genetics.**
- Eight recurrent missense and nonsense variants (for example R168X, R255X, R270X, R294X, R106W, R133C, T158M, R306C) account for roughly 60 to 70% of cases. C-terminal truncations are another recurrent class.
- Genotype correlates with severity. R133C and R294X tend to be milder, and R168X and R255X more severe.
- Skewed X-inactivation in a carrier can produce a mild phenotype or none at all.
- The **MECP2 duplication syndrome** in males shows that too much protein is also harmful. The gene is dosage-sensitive.

**Neuropathology** shows small, densely packed neurons with reduced dendritic arbors and spines, but no neurodegeneration. This fits a disorder of neuronal maturation and maintenance rather than cell death.
levels.phd:
MeCP2's binding specificity has been extended beyond symmetric mCG. In mature neurons, **non-CG methylation (mCA)** builds up postnatally and is deposited by DNMT3A during the first years of life. MeCP2 binds mCA with high affinity. Gabel et al. (2015) and Lagger et al. (2017) showed that MeCP2 preferentially represses **long genes** (over 100 kb) in proportion to their intragenic mCA density. The resulting transcriptional changes are subtle (often below 1.5-fold) but spread across thousands of genes. This explains why candidate-gene hunts largely failed. RTT looks like a disorder of genome-wide fine-tuning rather than misregulation of a single target.

**Minimal functional protein.** Tillotson et al. (2017, Bird lab) built a mini-MeCP2 containing only the MBD and NID. It largely rescued Mecp2-null mice. Most pathogenic missense variants cluster in the MBD (R106W, R133C, T158M, which disrupt DNA binding) or the NID (R306C, which disrupts NCoR binding). This convergence supports a model in which MeCP2 acts as a **bridge** between methylated DNA and the co-repressor. The older model of MeCP2 as an activator (Chahrour et al., 2008), along with roles in splicing and chromatin compaction, remains debated. Some apparent activation may be indirect.

**Cell-type logic.** Conditional knockouts break down the phenotype by cell type:
- Deletion from GABAergic neurons (Chao et al., 2010) recapitulates most RTT features, including stereotypies and respiratory dysfunction.
- Brainstem and other circuit-specific deletions map the breathing abnormalities.
- Glial loss contributes through astrocytes and microglia, although the microglial findings have been contested.

**Reversibility.** Guy et al. (2007) used a Lox-Stop allele with tamoxifen-inducible Cre to re-express Mecp2 in symptomatic adult mice. This produced robust reversal of phenotypes. It showed that neurons are not permanently damaged and that MeCP2 is needed continuously for adult circuit function.

**Dosage.** Overexpression of about 2-fold (Collins et al., 2004) causes progressive neurological disease, mirroring the human duplication syndrome. Sztainberg et al. (2015) reversed duplication phenotypes in adult mice with antisense oligonucleotides. This narrow therapeutic window is the central problem for gene replacement in RTT.

**Synaptic physiology.** Null mice show reduced cortical excitatory drive, altered excitation/inhibition balance, impaired LTP, and reduced BDNF signaling. IGF-1 pathway deficits motivated the trofinetide program.
levels.expert:
**Therapeutics.** In March 2023, the FDA approved **trofinetide** (Daybue). It is a synthetic analog of glypromate (glycine-proline-glutamate), the N-terminal tripeptide of IGF-1, and it is the first disease-specific RTT therapy. In the phase 3 LAVENDER trial, it modestly improved the Rett Syndrome Behaviour Questionnaire and Clinical Global Impression co-primary endpoints. Diarrhea and vomiting were frequent and caused many discontinuations. Its mechanism is incompletely defined, and clinicians debate how meaningful the benefit is.

**Gene therapy** must solve the dosage problem. In an X-mosaic brain, delivering MECP2 everywhere would overdose the roughly half of cells already expressing a normal allele. Strategies include:
- **Self-regulating cassettes**, such as Neurogene's NGN-401 using EXACT microRNA-based feedback and Taysha's TSHA-102 with miRARE. Both are in early-phase intrathecal or intracerebroventricular trials.
- **Reactivation of the silent X** (inhibiting XIST or DNA methylation) to unmask the wild-type allele. Off-target X reactivation is a concern.
- **RNA editing** (ADAR recruitment) or base editing to correct C>T nonsense variants such as R168X and R255X.
- **Read-through** compounds for nonsense alleles. Efficacy has been limited so far.

**Clinical pitfalls.**
- Regression around 18 months is often first labeled autism. Loss of hand use, stereotypies and slowing head growth should prompt MECP2 testing.
- Breath-holding and hyperventilation episodes can be mistaken for seizures. Video-EEG prevents unnecessary antiseizure escalation.
- **Prolonged QTc** and autonomic instability contribute to sudden death. Baseline and periodic ECGs are recommended, and QT-prolonging drugs should be avoided.
- Multidisciplinary care covers scoliosis (often surgical), osteopenia, GI dysmotility and feeding, gallbladder disease, and **eye-gaze communication devices**. Receptive understanding is often greater than it appears.
- In **males**, MECP2 variants range from neonatal encephalopathy to milder intellectual disability with psychiatric features. Somatic mosaicism and Klinefelter (XXY) karyotype can produce classic RTT.

**Open questions.** Which outcome measures detect meaningful change? Natural history studies are informing new scales. Is there a developmental window for treatment, given that mouse rescue works in adults? And how much of the phenotype arises from the brainstem and periphery rather than the cortex?

keyPoints: Rett syndrome: normal early development, then regression of speech and hand use
Caused mainly by de novo MECP2 mutations on the X chromosome
Mostly affects girls because of X-inactivation mosaicism
MeCP2 binds methylated DNA and recruits the NCoR/SMRT co-repressor
Restoring Mecp2 in adult mice reversed symptoms (Guy et al., 2007)
MECP2 is dosage-sensitive; trofinetide is the first approved RTT drug

test.q: Which gene is mutated in about 95% of classic Rett syndrome cases?
test.explain: MECP2 on Xq28 is the cause of nearly all classic cases. CDKL5 and FOXG1 cause related atypical forms.

test.q: What is the typical early course of Rett syndrome?
choices: Seizures as the first and main sign
Steady decline like dementia into adulthood
Delays that are obvious from birth
test.explain: Development appears normal for about 6 to 18 months, then skills regress and later stabilize. It is not a continuous decline.

test.q: Why is Rett syndrome seen mostly in girls?
choices: Boys recover from the disorder in infancy
The gene is on the Y chromosome
test.explain: Females have healthy and mutant cells because of random X-inactivation. Males with severe variants usually have a more serious infantile encephalopathy.

test.q: Which is a hallmark motor sign of Rett syndrome?
choices: Tremor of the head at rest
Tics of the face and shoulders
test.explain: Hand stereotypies such as wringing, clapping or mouthing replace purposeful hand use.

test.q: MeCP2 mainly binds to which kind of DNA?
test.explain: The methyl-CpG-binding domain recognizes methylated cytosines, including mCA in neurons.

test.q: Which co-repressor complex does MeCP2 recruit through its NID?
test.explain: The NCoR/SMRT interaction domain binds the co-repressor complex containing HDAC3.

test.q: What did Guy et al. (2007) show in Rett mice?
choices: Neurons died in large numbers early on
Symptoms began before birth in mice
test.explain: Re-expressing Mecp2 in symptomatic adult mice reversed many phenotypes, showing that neurons were not permanently damaged.

test.q: What does MECP2 duplication syndrome in males demonstrate?
choices: The gene is located on chromosome 15
test.explain: Both too little and too much MeCP2 cause disease, so the gene is dosage-sensitive.

test.q: What does Rett syndrome neuropathology mainly show?
choices: Widespread loss of neurons in the cortex
Large tubers in the cerebral cortex
Small neurons with fewer dendritic spines
test.explain: Neurons are small and densely packed with reduced dendrites, without neurodegeneration.

test.q: What term describes a mutation that is new in the child and not inherited from a parent?
test.explain: Most Rett mutations are de novo and usually arise in the paternal germline.

test.q: The random silencing of one X chromosome in each female cell is called X-___.
test.explain: X-inactivation creates mosaicism, which explains the sex difference and variable severity.

test.q: Which drug, an IGF-1 tripeptide analog, was FDA-approved for Rett syndrome in 2023?
test.explain: Trofinetide (Daybue) is the first Rett-specific approved therapy.

kidTest.q: When do children with Rett syndrome start losing skills?
choices: On the day they are born
kidTest.explain: They develop normally at first, then lose some skills around age 1 to 2.

kidTest.q: What do the hands often do in Rett syndrome?
choices: Stay still for most of the day
kidTest.explain: The hands make repeated movements like washing or clapping.

kidTest.q: Who gets Rett syndrome most often?
kidTest.explain: It mostly affects girls.

kidTest.q: What does the MECP2 helper act like in brain cells?
choices: A volume knob for other genes
kidTest.explain: It turns many other genes up or down, like a volume knob.

kidTest.q: A gene is like a recipe ___ in your cells. (c _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: Genes are like recipe cards that tell cells what to make.

advancedTest.q: Why did hunts for a single key MeCP2 target gene largely fail?
choices: Small changes across thousands of long genes produce the phenotype together
MeCP2 binds DNA in ways unrelated to methylation
Target genes are expressed mainly in the fetal brain before symptoms
MeCP2 is expressed mainly in glia rather than in neurons
advancedTest.explain: MeCP2 fine-tunes many long, mCA-rich genes with small fold changes, so no single target explains the disorder.

advancedTest.q: The rescue by mini-MeCP2 (MBD plus NID) best supports which model?
choices: MeCP2 acts mainly as a splicing factor in neurons
MeCP2 works mainly by compacting the mitochondrial genome
MeCP2 directly activates transcription of BDNF alone
MeCP2 bridges methylated DNA to the NCoR/SMRT co-repressor
advancedTest.explain: Keeping only the DNA-binding and co-repressor-binding domains was enough to rescue mice, and missense variants cluster in those two domains.

advancedTest.q: Why is unregulated MECP2 gene replacement risky in affected girls?
choices: The viral vector fails to reach brainstem neurons
The transgene would silence the healthy X chromosome
Cells already expressing the wild-type allele could be overdosed
Girls lack the receptor needed for viral entry
advancedTest.explain: Because of X-mosaicism, about half the cells already make normal MeCP2. Extra copies there could mimic duplication syndrome, which is why self-regulating cassettes are used.

advancedTest.q: A girl carries a severe MECP2 truncation yet has only mild features. What is the likeliest explanation?
choices: The mutation was inherited on her father's X chromosome
A coexisting CDKL5 variant offsets the MECP2 defect
Most cells inactivate the normal X, leaving the mutant X active
Most cells inactivate the mutant X, leaving the normal X active
advancedTest.explain: Females are mosaic for X-inactivation. If skewing preferentially silences the mutant X, most cells express normal MeCP2, which softens the phenotype. The opposite skew would worsen it. Paternal origin of the mutation (typical of de novo MECP2 changes) does not explain mildness. A CDKL5 variant would not compensate for loss of MeCP2.

lessons.title: Tuberous Sclerosis Complex and mTOR Signaling

levels.kid:
Inside every cell is a little "grow" switch called **mTOR**. When it is on, the cell gets bigger and builds more parts. Two helper proteins, called **TSC1** and **TSC2**, act like brakes on that switch.

In **tuberous sclerosis complex**, a child is born with a broken brake gene. Most of the time the other copy still works. But in some cells the second brake breaks too, and the grow switch stays stuck on. Those cells grow into lumps, like little extra bumps in the brain, skin, heart and kidneys.

The brain bumps can cause seizures and trouble with learning. The good news: scientists found medicines that press on the grow switch from the outside, which helps shrink some lumps.
levels.hs:
**Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)** is a genetic disorder caused by a harmful change (mutation) in one of two genes: **TSC1**, which makes a protein called hamartin, or **TSC2**, which makes tuberin. It affects roughly 1 in 6,000 births. It is **autosomal dominant**, but about two-thirds of cases are new mutations, not inherited from a parent.

The TSC proteins work together as a brake on **mTOR** (mechanistic target of rapamycin), a master regulator that tells cells to grow and make proteins when nutrients and growth signals are present. Without the brake, mTOR is overactive and cells grow too large and disorganized.

This produces **hamartomas**, benign growths made of a tissue's own cells arranged abnormally. In TSC they appear in many organs:
- **Brain**: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, and SEGAs (subependymal giant cell astrocytomas)
- **Skin**: facial angiofibromas and pale "ash-leaf" spots
- **Heart**: rhabdomyomas, often seen before birth
- **Kidney**: angiomyolipomas

The brain effects matter most for daily life. Most people with TSC have **epilepsy**, often starting in infancy with **infantile spasms**. Many also have intellectual disability or autism. Together these behavioral and psychiatric problems are called **TAND** (TSC-Associated Neuropsychiatric Disorders).

Example: a baby with a heart rhabdomyoma on prenatal ultrasound is screened for TSC, then watched closely for seizures.
levels.college:
TSC is a model disease because a single pathway, **mTORC1**, explains most of its features.

**The pathway.**
- Growth factors activate PI3K, then **AKT**, which phosphorylates and inhibits TSC2.
- TSC1, TSC2 and **TBC1D7** form the TSC complex. TSC2 is a **GTPase-activating protein (GAP)** for the small GTPase **Rheb**, switching Rheb-GTP to inactive Rheb-GDP.
- Rheb-GTP activates **mTORC1** at the lysosome, where amino acids also recruit mTORC1 through Rag GTPases.
- mTORC1 phosphorylates **S6K** and **4E-BP1**, boosting translation and ribosome production, and it suppresses **autophagy**.
- AMPK, active when energy is low, activates TSC2, linking growth to energy status.

Loss of TSC function means Rheb stays GTP-bound and mTORC1 runs constitutively. A useful marker is **phospho-S6** staining in lesions.

**Genetics.** TSC2 mutations are more common in sporadic cases and usually cause more severe disease than TSC1 mutations. The contiguous **TSC2/PKD1** deletion on chromosome 16p13.3 adds severe early polycystic kidney disease. Lesions often show a **second hit** (Knudson model) that knocks out the remaining allele.

**Neuropathology.**
- **Cortical tubers**: disorganized lamination, dysmorphic neurons and **giant cells** (balloon cells), resembling focal cortical dysplasia type IIb.
- **Subependymal nodules** along the ventricles, some growing into **SEGAs** near the foramen of Monro, which can block CSF flow and cause hydrocephalus.

**Clinical neurology.** About 80-90% develop epilepsy. Infantile spasms are common and are treated first-line with **vigabatrin** in TSC. Early seizure control correlates with better cognitive outcome.

**Therapy.** The rapalogs **sirolimus (rapamycin)** and **everolimus** bind FKBP12 and inhibit mTORC1. Everolimus shrinks SEGAs and renal angiomyolipomas and reduces refractory seizures. Topical sirolimus treats facial angiofibromas.
levels.phd:
Molecularly, the TSC complex is a heterotrimer in which TSC2's C-terminal GAP domain provides catalytic activity toward Rheb. TSC1 stabilizes TSC2 against ubiquitin-mediated degradation, and TBC1D7 stabilizes the complex. Much regulation is spatial: insulin/AKT phosphorylation of TSC2 (S939, T1462) promotes its release from the lysosomal surface, freeing Rheb to activate mTORC1. Amino acid sensing converges separately through Rag heterodimers and the Ragulator. This explains why mTORC1 needs both growth factor and nutrient inputs.

mTORC1 (mTOR, Raptor, mLST8) is distinct from **mTORC2** (Rictor, mSIN1), which phosphorylates AKT S473 and regulates the cytoskeleton. In TSC-null cells, S6K-mediated negative feedback on IRS1 dampens PI3K-AKT signaling. This feedback partly explains why hamartomas are rarely malignant. Rapalogs relieve the feedback, which can reactivate AKT and limit their antitumor effect; being largely cytostatic, they let tumors regrow when stopped. Rapamycin-FKBP12 inhibits mTORC1 allosterically and incompletely, sparing some 4E-BP1 phosphorylation.

The **second-hit** question in the brain is still debated. SEGAs and angiomyolipomas regularly show biallelic loss, but tubers often do not show a detectable somatic second hit. Deep sequencing has found low-frequency second hits in some tubers. This suggests tubers can arise from a small biallelic clone acting on neighboring cells, or from haploinsufficiency in a vulnerable progenitor. Timing matters: tuber cells resemble outer radial glia, implying a mid-gestational origin.

Mouse models clarified pathogenesis. Synapsin-Cre or GFAP-Cre Tsc1 conditional knockouts develop seizures, megalencephaly and enlarged neurons, and rapamycin rescues survival (Zeng et al., 2008; Meikle et al., 2008). Heterozygous Tsc2+/- mice lack lesions yet show learning deficits rescued by rapamycin in adulthood (Ehninger et al., 2008). This suggested that some cognitive impairment is a reversible, ongoing signaling problem rather than a fixed structural one. Neuronal consequences include excess protein synthesis, impaired axon guidance, reduced autophagic spine pruning (increased spine density; Tang et al., 2014) and altered mGluR-LTD, linking TSC to Fragile X as opposing ends of a synaptic protein-synthesis axis. Human iPSC cortical organoids now model the biallelic hits.

Genotype-phenotype is imperfect. About 10-15% of patients meeting clinical criteria have no mutation identified by conventional testing (NMI). Many of these have mosaic or deep intronic TSC2 variants.
levels.expert:
Diagnosis uses the 2021 International TSC Consensus criteria. A pathogenic TSC1/TSC2 variant alone is diagnostic. Otherwise two major features, or one major plus two or more minor features, are needed. The 2021 update grouped tubers and other cortical dysplasias into a single "multiple cortical tubers and/or radial migration lines" feature. Pitfall: renal angiomyolipoma plus lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) together count as only one major feature, because both occur in sporadic LAM. Fetal cardiac rhabdomyomas carry a high positive predictive value, making prenatal detection a common entry point.

The most clinically important advance is **preventive epilepsy treatment**. EPISTOP (2021) monitored infants with serial EEG and started vigabatrin when epileptiform discharges appeared, before clinical seizures. This delayed seizure onset and reduced drug-resistant epilepsy. The US PREVeNT trial gave more nuanced results, with a weaker effect on developmental outcome. Whether pre-emptive treatment truly improves cognition, rather than just delaying seizures, remains the central open question. Vigabatrin's retinal toxicity (visual field loss) needs monitoring, although it is hard to test in infants.

For drug-resistant epilepsy:
- **Everolimus** (EXIST-3) reduced focal seizure frequency.
- **Cannabidiol** gained approval for TSC seizures. Note its interaction with everolimus, which raises everolimus blood levels, so levels must be monitored.
- **Epilepsy surgery**: many patients have several tubers, but MEG, high-density EEG, FDG-PET and stereo-EEG can locate a dominant epileptogenic tuber. Resection or laser interstitial thermal therapy can achieve seizure freedom. Multifocality is not an absolute contraindication.

SEGA management is a classic neurosurgical decision. Growing or symptomatic SEGAs near the foramen of Monro can be resected, often more easily when small. Everolimus is the alternative, but it needs indefinite therapy because SEGAs regrow when it is stopped. Surveillance MRI is recommended every 1-3 years until about age 25.

TAND is underrecognized. Formal screening with the TAND Checklist at each visit is recommended. Everolimus trials have not shown clear cognitive or autism benefits in children and adults, which suggests the developmental window or the structural lesions limit how much can be reversed later. Research directions include brain-penetrant mTORC1-selective inhibitors, and lesion-specific somatic sequencing to resolve tuber biology.

The TSC complex is a GAP for Rheb and brakes mTORC1
Loss of the brake causes hamartomas in brain, skin, heart and kidney
Brain lesions: cortical tubers, subependymal nodules and SEGAs
Most patients have epilepsy; vigabatrin is first-line for infantile spasms
Rapalogs (everolimus, sirolimus) inhibit mTORC1 and shrink lesions

lessons.title: NF1 and the RASopathies

levels.kid:
Inside every cell there is a little message line, like a doorbell wire. When a growth signal rings the bell, a switch called **RAS** turns on and tells the cell, "Grow! Divide!"

A good switch also turns off again. A helper protein called **neurofibromin** is the hand that flips RAS back off.

Some children are born with a broken copy of the gene for neurofibromin. This condition is called **NF1**. The RAS switch stays on too long. Kids with NF1 often have light brown spots on their skin, called café-au-lait spots. They can get soft bumps called neurofibromas. Many have trouble paying attention or learning.

Doctors watch these kids carefully. New medicines can help turn the overactive signal down.
levels.hs:
**Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)** is one of the most common single-gene disorders. It affects about 1 in 3,000 people. It is **autosomal dominant**, so one faulty copy of the **NF1** gene on chromosome 17 is enough to cause it. About half of cases are new mutations that neither parent carries.

The NF1 gene makes **neurofibromin**. Neurofibromin switches off **RAS**, a protein that passes growth signals from the cell surface to the nucleus. RAS is on when it holds a molecule called GTP. It is off when it holds GDP. Neurofibromin speeds up the change from GTP to GDP. Without enough neurofibromin, RAS stays on, and cells grow and signal too much.

Common features include:
- **Café-au-lait spots** and freckles in the armpits or groin
- **Neurofibromas**, which are benign tumors of nerve sheaths
- **Lisch nodules**, small spots on the iris
- **Optic pathway gliomas**, slow tumors along the optic nerve
- Learning problems and ADHD, which affect roughly half of children

NF1 belongs to a larger family called the **RASopathies**. These are genetic syndromes caused by mutations in the same RAS pathway. One example is **Noonan syndrome**, often caused by mutations in PTPN11. It causes heart defects, short stature and distinctive facial features.
levels.college:
The **RAS-MAPK pathway** links growth-factor receptors to the nucleus. A receptor tyrosine kinase activates adaptors (GRB2) and the exchange factor **SOS1**, which loads RAS with GTP. Active RAS recruits **RAF**, which phosphorylates **MEK1/2**, which phosphorylates **ERK1/2**. ERK then alters transcription, translation and synaptic proteins. RAS also activates PI3K-AKT-mTOR.

**Neurofibromin** is a RAS **GTPase-activating protein (GAP)**. RAS hydrolyses GTP very slowly by itself; the GAP domain of neurofibromin inserts an "arginine finger" that speeds hydrolysis enormously. Loss of neurofibromin therefore raises RAS-GTP.

**Tumors follow Knudson's two-hit model.** Patients inherit one mutant allele in every cell. Tumors such as plexiform neurofibromas arise when Schwann cells lose the second allele. They also need a supportive microenvironment, notably NF1-heterozygous mast cells.

**Cognition is a haploinsufficiency effect.** No second hit is needed for learning problems. Key findings:
- Nf1+/- mice show deficits in spatial learning and in long-term potentiation (LTP).
- Excess RAS-ERK in inhibitory interneurons raises GABA release, damping LTP.

**Other RASopathies** share features such as heart defects, short stature, facial differences and variable intellectual disability:
- **Noonan syndrome**: PTPN11 (SHP2, about 50%), SOS1, RAF1, RIT1, KRAS
- **Costello syndrome**: HRAS
- **Cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome**: BRAF, MEK1/2, KRAS
- **Legius syndrome**: SPRED1, an NF1-like phenotype with café-au-lait spots but no neurofibromas

Most RASopathy mutations are activating (gain of function). NF1 instead loses a brake. Both routes produce the same result: too much signaling through the pathway.

**Therapy:** the MEK inhibitor **selumetinib** was FDA-approved in 2020 for children with symptomatic, inoperable plexiform neurofibromas.
levels.phd:
Neurofibromin is a ~2,818-residue protein whose central **GAP-related domain (GRD)** stimulates RAS GTP hydrolysis by orders of magnitude via the catalytic Arg1276. Recent cryo-EM structures show neurofibromin forms a high-affinity **dimer**, with the GRD and the Sec14-PH module packed in autoinhibited and open conformations. This hints at regulation beyond simple catalysis. SPRED1 binds the GRD and recruits neurofibromin to the membrane, which explains the overlap with Legius syndrome.

The **learning phenotype** is a model case of mechanism-driven translation. Silva and colleagues (Costa et al., Nature 2002) showed that Nf1+/- mice have spatial learning deficits and impaired hippocampal LTP. Both were rescued by reducing Ras activity, either genetically (Kras heterozygosity) or pharmacologically, including with farnesyltransferase inhibitors and later the statin lovastatin (Li et al., 2005), which lowers Ras isoprenylation. Cui et al. (Cell 2008) localized the defect to inhibitory neurons. Deleting Nf1 in interneurons alone raised ERK-dependent synapsin I phosphorylation and GABA release. Deleting it in excitatory neurons did not.

Neurofibromin also positively regulates **cAMP** through adenylyl cyclase. In Drosophila, Nf1 loss impairs learning in a cAMP-dependent manner. In mice, cAMP reduction contributes to optic glioma growth and retinal ganglion cell death. So the phenotype is not purely a RAS effect.

Tumor biology needs a second hit plus a permissive niche. Zhu et al. (Science 2002) showed that plexiform neurofibromas require Nf1-/- Schwann-lineage cells within an Nf1+/- environment. The heterozygous mast cells respond to Schwann-cell **SCF/c-kit** signaling. Optic gliomas similarly depend on microglia and on neuronal activity. Visual experience drives release of NLGN3 and a midkine-dependent T cell-microglia axis (Pan et al., Nature 2021).

The RASopathies show that a pathway's **dosage and kinetics**, rather than on/off logic, set phenotypes. Germline gain-of-function variants are hypomorphic compared with oncogenic somatic ones. Germline HRAS G12S is tolerated, while strongly transforming alleles are embryonic lethal. PTPN11 is a striking example. Gain-of-function causes Noonan syndrome, while catalytically impaired variants cause Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines, yet both raise MAPK output in some tissues. Genotype-phenotype correlations within NF1 are rare. Exceptions include the c.2970_2972delAAT (p.Met992del) deletion, which gives a mild phenotype without neurofibromas, and whole-gene microdeletions, which bring a heavier tumor burden and lower IQ.
levels.expert:
**Diagnosis.** The 2021 revised NF1 criteria (Legius et al.) added genetic confirmation and choroidal abnormalities. A child who has only café-au-lait spots now needs testing that can separate NF1 from **Legius syndrome**, because Legius does not need tumor surveillance. Constitutional **mismatch repair deficiency** can also mimic NF1 pigmentation and carries a severe cancer risk, so consider it if the family history suggests it. Mosaic (segmental) NF1 may yield negative blood testing. Testing affected tissue, such as café-au-lait melanocytes or tumor, can resolve it.

**Neurosurgical relevance.**
- Optic pathway gliomas occur in ~15% of children with NF1 but often stay indolent. Surveillance relies on ophthalmological exams rather than routine screening MRI. Treatment is reserved for progression or vision loss, typically with chemotherapy. Radiation is avoided because of secondary malignancy and moyamoya.
- **Moyamoya vasculopathy**, aqueductal stenosis, spinal neurofibromas causing cord compression, and sphenoid wing dysplasia all reach neurosurgeons.
- **Malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors (MPNST)** carry a ~8-13% lifetime risk. A painful, rapidly enlarging or hard plexiform lesion needs assessment. FDG-PET and a precursor called ANNUBP (atypical neurofibroma) guide biopsy. Progression involves CDKN2A loss, then PRC2 (SUZ12/EED) loss.
- T2 hyperintensities on MRI ("focal areas of signal intensity") are common and usually benign. Do not mistake them for tumor.

**Therapy beyond selumetinib.** **Mirdametinib** was approved in 2025 for adults and children with symptomatic plexiform neurofibromas. MEK inhibitors also shrink low-grade gliomas, though tumors often regrow after stopping. Toxicities include acneiform rash, paronychia, CK elevation and, rarely, cardiac or retinal effects. Combining MEK inhibitors with SHP2 or mTOR inhibitors is under study.

**Cognition remains unsolved.** The mouse lovastatin rescue did not translate: randomized trials of lovastatin and simvastatin in children with NF1 failed to improve cognition. Possible reasons include a narrow developmental window, poor CNS target engagement, and outcome measures insensitive to change. Trials of MEK inhibitors and of the GABA-B antagonists and dopamine strategies suggested by animal work are being explored. Many children have ADHD, which responds to standard ADHD therapies.

**Open questions:** why identical germline variants yield highly variable expressivity within families (modifier genes, stochastic second hits), and whether early RAS-pathway modulation can alter neurodevelopmental trajectories in Noonan syndrome and CFC syndrome.

lessons.title: SHANK3 and Phelan-McDermid Syndrome

levels.kid:
Brain cells talk to each other at tiny meeting spots called **synapses**. On the receiving side of each synapse there is a busy little platform that holds the cell's "ears" in the right place.

A protein called **SHANK3** is like the scaffolding that holds that platform together. It is a bit like the frame of a bunk bed: it keeps all the pieces connected.

Some children are born missing one of their two copies of the SHANK3 instructions. This is called **Phelan-McDermid syndrome**. With only half the scaffolding, the platforms are wobbly, so brain messages get through less well.

These kids may learn to talk late or not much, and many have autism. They often have soft, floppy muscles and may not feel pain as much. Doctors and families help them learn and grow.
levels.hs:
**Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS)**, also called **22q13 deletion syndrome**, is a genetic condition caused by losing one working copy of the gene **SHANK3**. SHANK3 sits near the very tip of the long arm (q arm) of chromosome 22. Some people have a small deletion that removes the end of the chromosome. Others have a change, called a **variant**, inside SHANK3 itself.

SHANK3 makes a **scaffolding protein** in the **postsynaptic density (PSD)**. The PSD is a dense protein patch just under the membrane of an excitatory synapse, the kind that uses the neurotransmitter **glutamate**. SHANK3 links glutamate receptors to other scaffold proteins and to the actin skeleton inside **dendritic spines**, the tiny bumps where synapses form.

Because losing one copy is enough to cause disease, PMS is an example of **haploinsufficiency**: half the normal amount of protein is not enough.

Common features:
- Moderate to profound intellectual disability
- Absent or severely delayed speech
- Autism (in roughly half to three-quarters of people)
- Low muscle tone (**hypotonia**) in infancy
- Reduced response to pain, and trouble controlling body temperature
- In teens and adults, a risk of mood problems and loss of skills (**regression**)

Most cases happen **de novo**, meaning the change is new in the child and not inherited. Diagnosis uses a **chromosomal microarray** or gene sequencing.
levels.college:
SHANK3 (SH3 and multiple ankyrin repeat domains 3) belongs to the **ProSAP/Shank** family (SHANK1-3). These are master scaffolds of the excitatory postsynaptic density.

**Domain architecture and binding partners:**
- N-terminal **SPN** domain and **ankyrin repeats**: bind Ras/Rap GTPases and the cytoskeletal protein alpha-fodrin
- **SH3 domain**: binds L-type calcium channel subunits
- **PDZ domain**: binds **SAPAP/GKAP**, which links to **PSD-95** and from there to NMDA receptors
- **Proline-rich region**: binds **Homer**, which couples to **mGluR1/5**, and binds **cortactin** and Abi-1, which act on actin
- **SAM domain**: self-multimerizes into zinc-dependent sheets that form a platform deep in the PSD

SHANK3 therefore bridges the NMDA receptor/PSD-95 complex, group I metabotropic glutamate receptors and the actin cytoskeleton. Through these links it shapes spine size, maturation and synaptic strength.

**Genetics of PMS:**
- Terminal 22q13.3 deletions range from under 100 kb to more than 9 Mb. They arise from simple deletions, unbalanced translocations or **ring chromosome 22**.
- **Pathogenic SHANK3 variants** (frameshift, nonsense) on their own reproduce the core neurodevelopmental phenotype.
- Larger deletions remove neighbouring genes and tend to bring more medical problems, such as kidney anomalies and lymphedema. However, the link between deletion size and severity is imperfect.

**Clinical spectrum:** neonatal hypotonia; global developmental delay; absent or minimal speech; autism; seizures in roughly a quarter to a third of patients; sleep disturbance; decreased pain sensitivity; and minor dysmorphic features such as long eyelashes, large fleshy hands and dysplastic toenails. Growth is usually normal or accelerated. This contrasts with many deletion syndromes, which cause short stature. Brain MRI may show thinning of the corpus callosum or delayed myelination.

SHANK3 variants also turn up in large autism and intellectual disability cohorts. SHANK3 is one of the most consistently implicated single genes in autism, accounting for roughly 0.5-1% of cases.
levels.phd:
**Discovery.** Phelan's group described 22q13 terminal deletions in the 1980s-90s. Bonaglia and colleagues (2001) mapped a translocation breakpoint that disrupted SHANK3/ProSAP2, which identified it as the critical gene. Durand et al. (2007) then reported SHANK3 mutations in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), placing a synaptic scaffold at the centre of autism genetics.

**Gene structure complicates models.** SHANK3 has 22 or more exons, several intragenic promoters and extensive alternative splicing. It produces multiple isoforms that differ in which domains they contain. Exon 21 encodes much of the proline-rich region and is a hotspot for truncating variants, including a G-rich stretch prone to frameshifts. The gene's high GC content impaired short-read sequencing coverage for years, which caused cases to be missed.

**Mouse models.** Peça et al. (2011, Feng lab) deleted exons 13-16 (PDZ). These mice showed self-injurious overgrooming, social deficits and corticostriatal dysfunction, with reduced striatal PSD size and lower SAPAP3/Homer levels. Other lines (ankyrin, SH3 or exon 21 deletions) produced divergent phenotypes because different isoforms survive in each. Only complete deletion of all isoforms approaches the human haploinsufficiency state. Key synaptic findings include:
- Reduced AMPA/NMDA-mediated transmission and impaired LTP in hippocampus and striatum
- Altered mGluR5-Homer coupling
- Fewer and immature dendritic spines, linked to failure of actin regulation through cortactin and the Rac1/PAK pathway
- HCN channel dysfunction (Yi et al. 2016, in human neurons)

**Developmental rescue.** Mei et al. (2016) built a Cre-dependent conditional knock-in to restore Shank3 in adult mice. Restoration rescued spine density, striatal transmission, social interaction and grooming, but not anxiety or motor deficits. This suggests some circuits keep their plasticity into adulthood. The result revived optimism that ASD-associated synaptic phenotypes can be reversed.

**Zinc.** The SAM domain needs Zn2+ to form sheets. Arons et al. linked synaptic zinc to Shank3-dependent postsynaptic maturation, which raised interest in zinc's role in the PSD.

**Open questions:** how a small change in the dose of a scaffold protein produces such a severe phenotype; why outcomes vary so much between patients; and whether pain hyporesponsivity comes from Shank3 in dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, where it regulates HCN and TRPV1.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic pitfalls.**
- Karyotype misses most terminal deletions, so a **chromosomal microarray** is first-line.
- When a microarray is normal and suspicion remains, request exome or genome sequencing. Ask the lab to confirm that SHANK3 coverage is adequate, especially across the GC-rich exons and exon 21.
- **Ring chromosome 22** carries a risk of NF2-related schwannomatosis and meningiomas. For a neurosurgeon, that makes neuro-oncologic vigilance part of lifelong care.
- Parental testing matters. A balanced translocation in a parent sharply raises the risk of recurrence, whereas de novo cases carry a low recurrence risk with a small chance of germline mosaicism.

**Clinical management** follows consensus guidelines (Srivastava et al. 2023 update). Key elements:
- Kidney ultrasound, cardiac evaluation and EEG when indicated
- Hearing and vision screening
- Monitoring for lymphedema
- Augmentative and alternative communication introduced early

Reduced pain reactivity means fractures, dental abscesses and appendicitis can present only as a behaviour change.

**Adolescent regression and psychiatric decompensation** are distinctive to PMS. Catatonia, bipolar-like episodes and loss of motor or self-care skills are reported in a substantial minority, with a peak in adolescence and young adulthood. Triggers may include infection or hormonal shifts. Recognizing catatonia matters because it is treatable. Clinicians need to separate it from seizures, depression and neurodegeneration.

**Therapeutic research.**
- **IGF-1** and **trofinetide-like** approaches: Kolevzon's group (Mount Sinai) ran small randomized pilot trials of recombinant IGF-1, building on the finding that IGF-1 rescues synaptic deficits in Shank3-deficient neurons. Signals for social withdrawal and restricted behaviour were encouraging but not definitive.
- **Oxytocin** and **intranasal insulin** trials produced mixed results.
- **Gene-dose restoration** is the logical goal. AAV delivery is hard because SHANK3 cDNA (about 5.2 kb) approaches packaging limits. Strategies include mini-SHANK3 constructs, dual vectors and CRISPR activation of the remaining allele. Overexpression is also a hazard: SHANK3 duplication causes manic-like behaviour in mice (Han et al. 2013) and is associated with bipolar disorder and ADHD in humans. This is an inverted-U dosage problem.

**Human models.** iPSC-derived neurons and cortical organoids from patients show reduced excitatory synaptic transmission and HCN deficits. Primate Shank3 models (macaque, marmoset) are being used to study social and sleep phenotypes.

**Open questions:** validated outcome measures and biomarkers, such as EEG and evoked potentials; why lithium appears helpful in some regressing patients; and the natural history in adults.

keyPoints: Phelan-McDermid syndrome results from loss of one SHANK3 copy at 22q13.3 (deletion or variant)
SHANK3 is a master scaffold of the excitatory postsynaptic density
It links PSD-95/GKAP/NMDA receptors, Homer/mGluR5 and the actin cytoskeleton in dendritic spines
Core features: hypotonia, absent speech, ID, autism, reduced pain response, normal growth
Adult Shank3 restoration in mice rescues some behaviors, so the disorder is partly reversible
SHANK3 dosage is inverted-U: duplication also causes disease, which complicates gene therapy

test.q: On which chromosome region is SHANK3 located?
test.explain: SHANK3 sits at the terminal end of chromosome 22's long arm, 22q13.3. Xq27.3 is FMR1, the fragile X gene.

test.q: Where in the neuron is SHANK3 protein mainly found?
test.explain: SHANK3 is a scaffold in the postsynaptic density of excitatory glutamatergic synapses.

test.q: Phelan-McDermid syndrome is caused by losing one gene copy. This mechanism is called:
test.explain: Half the normal amount of SHANK3 protein is not enough. That is haploinsufficiency.

test.q: Which SHANK3 domain binds Homer, which couples to mGluR5?
test.explain: The proline-rich region binds Homer and cortactin. The PDZ domain binds SAPAP/GKAP instead.

test.q: Which feature is typical of Phelan-McDermid syndrome?
test.explain: Absent or minimal speech is a core feature. Growth is usually normal or accelerated, and pain response is reduced.

test.q: What is the recommended first-line genetic test for a suspected 22q13 deletion?
test.explain: A microarray detects terminal deletions that a karyotype often misses.

test.q: SHANK3's SAM domain is notable because it:
choices: Anchors SHANK3 into the axonal membrane
test.explain: The SAM domain self-assembles into Zn2+-dependent sheets that form a platform deep in the PSD.

test.q: Most Phelan-McDermid cases arise:
choices: De novo in the affected child
test.explain: Most cases are new (de novo). A minority come from a parent's balanced translocation.

test.q: In SHANK3-deficient models, dendritic spines tend to be:
test.explain: Losing SHANK3 impairs actin regulation, which leads to fewer and less mature spines.

test.q: Low muscle tone, common in infants with PMS, is called ___.
test.explain: Neonatal hypotonia is often one of the first signs.

test.q: What is the other common name for Phelan-McDermid syndrome, based on its chromosome location?
test.explain: PMS is also called 22q13 deletion syndrome.

test.q: SHANK3 works at excitatory synapses that use the neurotransmitter ___.
test.explain: The postsynaptic density SHANK3 organizes belongs to glutamatergic synapses.

kidTest.q: What is a synapse?
choices: A spot where brain cells talk
A tiny bone found inside the ear
A type of cell that floats in blood
kidTest.explain: Synapses are the meeting spots where brain cells send messages.

kidTest.q: What job does the SHANK3 protein do?
choices: It holds the synapse platform together
It carries oxygen around in the blood
It makes the hair on your head grow
kidTest.explain: SHANK3 is like scaffolding that keeps the receiving platform connected.

kidTest.q: Kids with Phelan-McDermid syndrome are missing:
kidTest.explain: They have only one working copy instead of two, so they have half the scaffolding.

kidTest.q: Which is common in kids with this syndrome?
kidTest.explain: Speech is often very delayed or absent.

kidTest.q: Kids with this syndrome often have soft, floppy m _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Low muscle tone makes muscles feel soft and floppy.

advancedTest.q: Why do different Shank3 knockout mouse lines show divergent phenotypes?
choices: Each line was raised on a different diet during development
The gene is X-linked, so sex effects dominate each line
Intragenic promoters let different isoforms survive in each deletion
SHANK3 is imprinted, so just the paternal allele is expressed
advancedTest.explain: Multiple intragenic promoters and splicing mean that deleting one domain spares isoforms lacking it. Only complete deletion mimics human haploinsufficiency.

advancedTest.q: Mei et al. (2016) restored Shank3 in adult mice. The partial rescue implies that:
choices: SHANK3 has no function after early childhood
Deficits arise from irreversible neuronal death
Some circuits stay plastic in adulthood while others do not
Each phenotype requires restoration before birth
advancedTest.explain: Social behavior, grooming and striatal synapses were rescued, but anxiety and motor deficits were not. This points to circuit-specific critical periods.

advancedTest.q: Gene replacement for PMS faces an inverted-U dosage concern because:
choices: Ring chromosome 22 blocks any vector integration
The SHANK3 gene is too short to express from AAV vectors
SHANK3 duplication causes manic-like and bipolar phenotypes
Extra SHANK3 protein is rapidly cleared by microglia
advancedTest.explain: Overexpression is also pathogenic, as shown in mice and in human duplications, so the delivered dose must stay near normal. The cDNA is actually near the AAV size limit, not too short.

advancedTest.q: An adult with PMS and ring chromosome 22 develops new focal deficits. Which concern is specifically raised by the ring?
advancedTest.explain: Ring 22 can cause loss of NF2 at 22q12, which predisposes to schwannomas and meningiomas.
